flaws.title: Initialized start tick is skipped unless start and end are in different bitmap words and the end tick is unaligned, so active liquidity is tracked incorrectly
flaws.sequence:
1. A pool has tickSpacing 10. Position A covers [0,30) and position B covers [-50,50), with equal liquidity L. The current tick is exactly 30, which is the upper bound of A and initialized with liquidityNet = -L. Uniswap active liquidity at tick 30 is L, from B only.
2. The attacker (or any top-of-block swapper) does a zero-for-one swap that ends at a tick in the same bitmap word, for example tick 5. Alternatively the swap ends on an aligned tick in another word.
3. afterSwap calls _zeroForOneDistributeTax, then initDown, then reset(30). startWordPos == endWordPos, so the else branch runs and _advanceToNextDown starts searching from compress(29). Tick 30 is never returned.
4. CompensationPriceFinder.getZeroForOne and _zeroForOneCreditRewards start from liquidity = L. They never subtract -L at tick 30. At tick 0 they subtract +L and get 0. With a single position the subtraction underflows and the swap reverts.
5. With the attacker-crafted setup from the known finding (attacker liquidity added to [t1-s, t1)), the attacker's liquidity is left out of the growth computation. The global growth per unit of liquidity is inflated, and the attacker withdraws far more rewards than owed, up to all reward funds.
flaws.impact: Top-of-block zero-for-one swaps either revert (DoS) or credit reward growth computed from the wrong active liquidity. An attacker can steal LP rewards.
flaws.known_finding: All rewards can be stolen due to incorrect active liquidity calculations when the current tick is an exact multiple of the tick spacing at the upper end of a liquidity range

requirement_breaks: reset fails point 4/5: when startTick is an initialized multiple of the tick spacing it is not returned by getNext whenever startTick and endTick share a bitmap word or endTick is aligned, so the summed liquidity does not equal the active liquidity at endTick.
